q: A 20-year-old man is seen by a psychiatrist in the outpatient clinic. During the history, the patient is asked to describe his mood. He answers by stating, "Good question, people often want to know about your mood and most of the time without understanding the salient underpinnings of mood, I remember my teacher had asked me a similar question and I had described it so well. You will be surprised to know that even my family members keep asking about it, almost daily and I tell them about what researches show. I describe it so well that people love to listen to it. I am sure I have answered your question well, though it's a bit extensive but I am happy now, so it's okay!" Which of the following psychiatric findings best describes his thought disorder?
explanation: A. Loose association means ideas slip between unrelated topics with no logical link. His thoughts stay connected to the question. B. Circumstantiality is excessive, irrelevant detail and detours, but the speaker finally reaches the point. He does, ending with "I am sure I have answered your question well". C. Neologism is the invention of new words. None are used. D. Tangentiality means drifting away and never returning to the point. He does return to it. E. Flight of ideas is rapid, pressured jumping between ideas linked by puns or clang associations. His speech is long-winded, not fragmented.

q: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar mood disorder has been stable on lithium for 2 years. For the past 3 months, she has been easily fatigued, more sensitive to cold, and excessively sleepy. Her hair is dry and brittle, and her face is puffy. Which of the following lab results will most likely be found?
options: The blunted cortisol response to ACTH
explanation: A. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism (fatigue, cold intolerance, somnolence, dry hair, puffy face) gives a raised TSH with low T4. B. Lithium is not hepatotoxic; raised LFTs are a concern with valproate or carbamazepine. C. Lithium causes a benign leukocytosis, not leukopenia (carbamazepine and clozapine cause leukopenia). D. A blunted cortisol response to ACTH suggests adrenal insufficiency, which does not fit this picture. E. Hypothyroidism raises cholesterol (hypercholesterolaemia), not lowers it.

q: Which of the following hormones is most commonly used in the adjuvant treatment of depression?
explanation: A. Progesterone has no established role as an antidepressant adjuvant. B. Cortisol excess is associated with depression; it is not a treatment. C. ACTH is not used to treat depression. D. Thyroid hormone augmentation (T3 liothyronine, or T4 levothyroxine as listed here) is the most commonly used hormonal adjuvant to antidepressants. E. Prolactin has no therapeutic role in depression.

q: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency room with the chief complaint that "the boys are following me." He also complains of hearing a voice telling him to hurt his enemy. He tells the examiner that God gives him special messages and power to remodel the world and he is blessed with the supreme energy and skills to materialize God's dream! Which of the following psychiatric findings best describes the last belief of this patient?
explanation: A. A fixed false belief of special powers and a divine mission to remodel the world is a grandiose delusion. B. An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus, not a belief. C. Loose association is a thought-form disorder, not a belief. D. An idea of reference is the belief that neutral events relate to oneself. The belief in question is about special powers. E. Clouding of consciousness is reduced awareness of the environment, which is not described.

q: A 21-year-old female patient with schizophreniform disorder was prescribed Haloperidol 3 months ago and complained of galactorrhea for the last month. Further history and assessment rule out the possibility of pregnancy or brain tumour. Which of the following tracts is most probably involved in this case?
explanation: A. The nigrostriatal tract is linked to extrapyramidal side effects, not galactorrhoea. B. The mesocortical tract is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms. C. The mesolimbic tract is linked to positive symptoms and the therapeutic effect. D. "Hypothalamic" is not one of the four classic dopamine pathways; the relevant hypothalamic-pituitary pathway is the tuberoinfundibular tract. E. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular tract removes dopamine's inhibition of prolactin, causing hyperprolactinaemia and galactorrhoea.

q: A 35-year-old female is seen by a psychiatrist in the emergency room after she is found walking in the middle of a busy road with no footwear on. During her interview, she is asked to explain and use the proverb, "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush". Which of the following best describes the cognitive functions being tested by this request?
explanation: A. Orientation is tested with person, place and time. B. Immediate memory is tested by repeating digits or words. C. Fund of knowledge is tested with general facts (capitals, leaders). D. Concentration is tested with serial sevens or spelling backwards. E. Interpreting proverbs tests abstract reasoning (abstract versus concrete thinking).

q: A 64-year-old man is admitted to the psychiatric unit after an unsuccessful suicide attempt. Following admission, he attempts to cut his wrists three times in the next 24 hours and refuses to eat or drink anything. He is scheduled to have electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) because he is so severely depressed that an antidepressant is deemed too slow-acting. Which of the following side effects is generally not associated with modified ECT?
explanation: A. Headache is a common post-ECT side effect. B. Transient tachycardia and palpitations occur from the autonomic surge. C. Anterograde amnesia is a common, usually transient effect. D. Modified ECT uses a muscle relaxant (succinylcholine) and anaesthesia, so vertebral and other fractures are now rare. E. Retrograde amnesia is a well-known cognitive effect of ECT.

q: A 32-year-old man presents to his physician with a slowly developing difficulty of movement and thinking. The patient tells the physician that his father had similar problems. His wife notes that the patient appears depressed and apathetic. On examination, the patient has involuntary choreoathetoid movements of his face, hands, and shoulders. Which of the following areas of the brain is likely to show atrophy with this disease?
explanation: A. This is Huntington's disease (autosomal dominant, chorea, dementia, depression), with atrophy of the striatum, especially the caudate nucleus. B. Frontal atrophy is typical of Pick's disease or frontotemporal dementia. C. White-matter damage fits Binswanger's disease or multiple sclerosis. D. Cerebellar atrophy fits spinocerebellar ataxias. E. The pituitary is not involved.

q: An 85-year-old woman with a dementing disorder dies in a motor vehicle accident. During the previous 6-8 years, her personality had dramatically changed and she had caused much embarrassment to her family due to her intrusive and inappropriate behavior. Postmortem brain examination and biopsy show frontoparietal atrophy, swollen neurons, amyloid plaques, and neurofibrillary tangles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A. Alzheimer's disease classically begins with memory loss, and plaques and tangles are its hallmark. This is the main alternative answer, but the stem stresses early personality change and disinhibition. B. Pick disease (frontotemporal dementia) presents with early personality change and disinhibition, with swollen (ballooned) neurons (Pick cells). Intended answer, but see flag. C. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is rapidly progressive with spongiform change; it does not last 6-8 years. D. B12 deficiency dementia is potentially reversible and has no plaques or tangles. E. HIV dementia is a subcortical dementia with multinucleated giant cells.

q: A 29-year-old alcoholic is brought to the emergency room after he was found unconscious in the street. He is hospitalized for dehydration and pneumonia. While being treated, he becomes acutely confused and agitated. On examination, he cannot move his eyes upward or to the right, and he is ataxic. Psychological pillow, visual hallucinations, and amnesia were also elicited. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A. Intoxication does not explain ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. B. Korsakoff syndrome alone is amnesia with confabulation, without acute ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. C. Alcohol delirium (DTs) follows withdrawal with autonomic hyperactivity and does not cause ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. D. Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia (Wernicke triad) with amnesia indicate Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome from thiamine deficiency. E. Seizures are not described.

q: A 29-year-old alcoholic is brought to the emergency room after he was found unconscious in the street. He is hospitalized for dehydration and pneumonia. While being treated, he becomes acutely confused and agitated. On examination, he cannot move his eyes upward or to the right, and he is ataxic. Psychological pillow, visual hallucinations, and amnesia were also elicited. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the patient in the vignette above?
explanation: A. Thiamine (vitamin B1), given parenterally and before any glucose, treats Wernicke's encephalopathy. B. Riboflavin (B2) is not the deficient vitamin. C. Haloperidol does not treat the cause and can lower the seizure threshold. D. Pantothenic acid (B5) is not involved. E. Pyridoxine (B6) is not involved.

q: A 33-year-old woman was referred to the Psychiatry unit following extensive gastrointestinal evaluations at CMW Emergency and two other medical centers, neither of which revealed the cause of her symptoms. On admission, her serum potassium concentration was 2.2 mEq/L, her blood urea nitrogen level was 40 mg/dL, and her creatinine level was 2.0 mg/dL. A stool examination revealed severe secretory diarrhea, and the alkalinization test for phenolphthalein was strongly positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A. Malingering needs an obvious external incentive, which is not described. B. In somatoform disorders symptoms are not intentionally produced. C. Borderline personality disorder is not defined by covert laxative use. D. Covert phenolphthalein (laxative) use to produce illness, with repeated unexplained workups, is factitious disorder. E. Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect.

q: Which of the following etiologies is most likely underlying the behavior of the woman in the vignette above?
explanation: A. In factitious disorder the aim is to assume the sick role to meet an internal psychological need, which is primary gain. B. Secondary gain means external benefits (money, avoiding duties), as in malingering. C. No psychotic features are described. D. Nothing suggests intellectual disability. E. Laxatives are not a drug of dependence sought for effect.

q: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency room by her roommate after the patient tells her that "the voices are telling me to kill the teacher." The roommate states the patient has been isolative and "odd" for the last 4 months but for the past 5 weeks, she has been hoarding food, talking to herself, and appearing very paranoid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
explanation: A. Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 month. B. Schizophrenia needs at least 6 months of illness including prodrome; here the total is about 4 months. C. Psychotic symptoms with total illness duration between 1 and 6 months (about 4 months) is schizophreniform disorder. D. Schizoaffective disorder needs prominent mood episodes, which are absent. E. Delusional disorder has non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations or disorganisation.

q: The patient becomes very agitated in the emergency room, screaming that the nurses were there to kill her and that she had to escape. She tried to strike one of the nurses before being restrained. Which of the following treatment options is recommended first?
explanation: A. Rapid tranquillisation of an acutely agitated psychotic patient uses IM haloperidol with a benzodiazepine. B. Clozapine is slowly titrated and is for treatment-resistant illness. C. A depot is for maintenance and acts too slowly. D. Mellaril (thioridazine) has no parenteral form and carries QT risk. E. Oral diazepam alone is inadequate and unreliable in a restrained, agitated patient.

q: The above patient was admitted and started on a daily dose of Trifluperazine 5 mg nocte. After discharge from the hospital, she was kept on a low dose of the medication for 6 weeks. She showed only a minimal response to the drug, even after it was raised to a moderate dosage level. Which of the following options is the next therapeutic step?
options: Give a high dose of fluphenazine
Give a low dose of Clozaril
Give a low dose of Haloperidol
Give a low dose of Olanzapine
answer: Give a low dose of Olanzapine
explanation: A. Switching to a high dose of another conventional agent adds no benefit and more side effects. B. Clozapine is reserved for failure of at least two adequate antipsychotic trials; she has had only one. C. Another first-generation antipsychotic is unlikely to do better than trifluoperazine. D. A depot addresses non-adherence, not poor response. E. After a poor response to one conventional antipsychotic, switch to a second-generation agent such as olanzapine.

q: Which of the following statements refers to the principle of beneficence in medical ethics?
options: Treat indigent patients without monetary compensation
Build the patient-doctor relationship on trust
explanation: A. Beneficence is the duty to act in the patient's best interest: prevent harm and promote well-being. B. "Do no harm" is non-maleficence. C. Pro bono care is charity or professional generosity, not the definition of beneficence. D. Universal healthcare relates to distributive justice. E. Trust relates to fidelity and the therapeutic alliance.

q: A 30-year-old man lost his father suddenly to an accident in 2010. Two years later, he developed a repetitive thought that harm would result to loved ones if he did not move or walk specially. He knows the idea is strange and silly, but he cannot stop thinking about it. Later he developed elaborate urges that involved stepping in a just right way. The process has become time-consuming and cumbersome. Going out in public by himself or with family has become an ordeal for him. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A. Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with appearance. B. Delusional disorder lacks insight; he knows the idea is silly. C. Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with insight, plus time-consuming compulsions and impairment, is OCD. D. Somatization disorder involves multiple unexplained physical complaints. E. Hypochondriasis is fear of having a serious illness.

q: A 30-year-old man lost his father suddenly to an accident in 2010. Two years later, he developed a repetitive thought that harm would result to loved ones if he did not move or walk specially. He knows the idea is strange and silly, but he cannot stop thinking about it. Later he developed elaborate urges that involved stepping in a just right way. The process has become time-consuming and cumbersome. Going out in public by himself or with family has become an ordeal for him. Which of the following treatment options is likely to be most beneficial for the above patient?
explanation: A. A depot antipsychotic is not a treatment for OCD. B. Oral antipsychotics are not first-line for OCD. C. Antipsychotics are only an augmenting strategy for resistant OCD. D. Fluoxetine (SSRI) is effective, but the combination is better for impairing OCD. E. An SSRI (fluoxetine) combined with CBT/exposure and response prevention is the most effective treatment.

q: A 25-year-old man presents because of excessive sleepiness. He states that for the past 4 months, he has become so sleepy that he must sleep, even when he is in the middle of an important meeting. These episodes occur daily and the patient must sleep for 10 to 20 minutes during each episode. The patient also says that on several occasions he has had a sudden loss of muscle tone during which his knees become weak and he drops to the floor. He remains conscious during these episodes. He denies any substance abuse or medical problems. The above-described disorder is a problem of which of the following phases of sleep?
explanation: A. NREM-1 is light transitional sleep and is not the site of the pathology. B. NREM-2 is not the abnormal stage here. C. NREM-3 (slow-wave sleep) is linked to sleepwalking and night terrors. D. NREM-4 is likewise slow-wave sleep, linked to parasomnias. E. Narcolepsy with cataplexy is a REM-sleep disorder: REM features (atonia) intrude into wakefulness.

q: A 25-year-old man presents because of excessive sleepiness. He states that for the past 4 months, he has become so sleepy that he must sleep, even when he is in the middle of an important meeting. These episodes occur daily and the patient must sleep for 10 to 20 minutes during each episode. The patient also says that on several occasions he has had a sudden loss of muscle tone during which his knees become weak and he drops to the floor. He remains conscious during these episodes. He denies any substance abuse or medical problems. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: A. Benzodiazepines ("Benzenediamine" in the paper is presumably a typo) are sedating and worsen sleepiness. B. Valproic acid is not used for narcolepsy. C. Lithium is not used for narcolepsy. D. Modafinil, a wakefulness-promoting agent, is the first-line treatment for narcolepsy (cataplexy may need an antidepressant or sodium oxybate). E. Nasal CPAP treats obstructive sleep apnoea, not narcolepsy.

q: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency room by police officers after he was found standing in the middle of a busy highway, naked, commanding the traffic to stop. In the emergency room, he is agitated and restless, with pressured speech and an elated affect. His mother reveals over the phone the presence of such behavioral problems in some other family members as well. She also revealed that her son has more than 4-5 such episodes in a year and he has never used any substance and is not on any medication currently. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A. Delirium has clouded consciousness and fluctuating attention, which is not described. B. Elated mood, pressured speech, agitation, disinhibition, a positive family history and recurrent episodes indicate bipolar disorder, manic episode (rapid cycling given 4-5 episodes a year). C. A mixed state needs concurrent depressive symptoms, which are absent. D. Cyclothymia has milder, subthreshold mood swings, not florid mania. E. Schizophrenia is not defined by elated affect and episodic mania.

q: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency room by police officers after he was found standing in the middle of a busy highway, naked, commanding the traffic to stop. In the emergency room, he is agitated and restless, with pressured speech and an elated affect. His mother reveals over the phone the presence of such behavioral problems in some other family members as well. She also revealed that her son has more than 4-5 such episodes in a year and he has never used any substance and is not on any medication currently. The resident on call decides to start this patient on medication to control this disease. Which of the following would be the drug of choice?
explanation: A. More than 4 episodes a year is rapid cycling, which responds better to valproate than to lithium. Intended answer, but see flag. B. Haloperidol controls acute agitation but is not the long-term mood stabiliser of choice. C. Carbamazepine is a second-line alternative. D. Lithium is the classic first-line mood stabiliser and the textbook "drug of choice" for bipolar disorder, but it is less effective in rapid cycling. E. An SSRI can precipitate mania and is not used.

q: The benzodiazepines' action depends on their interaction with which of the following receptors?
explanation: A. Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the GABA-A receptor, increasing chloride channel opening frequency. B. Serotonin receptors are the target of buspirone and antidepressants. C. NMDA is the target of ketamine and memantine. D. Dopamine receptors are the target of antipsychotics. E. Acetylcholine is not the benzodiazepine target.

q: A 21-year-old newlywed female is brought to the emergency room by her husband after she woke up with paralysis of her right arm. The patient reports that the day before, she had gotten into a verbal altercation with her sister-in-law over her intrusiveness in their interpersonal life. The patient notes that from the beginning she had mixed feelings about her sister-in-law. Which of the following diagnoses best fits this patient's clinical picture?
explanation: A. No depressive syndrome is described. B. Acute neurological deficit (arm paralysis) after an emotional conflict, with no organic cause described, is conversion disorder. C. Histrionic personality disorder is an enduring pattern of attention-seeking, not an acute deficit. D. A fugue state is unexpected travel with amnesia for identity. E. Adjustment disorder gives emotional or behavioural symptoms, not a motor deficit.

q: Which of the following is not a function of the parietal lobes of the brain?
explanation: A. Tactile sensation is a core parietal function (somatosensory cortex). B. Visuospatial function is parietal (especially right). C. Prosody is not a parietal function: receptive (sensory) prosody is a function of the temporal lobe and motor prosody of the frontal lobe, so this is the exception. D. Reading is a dominant parietal (angular gyrus) function. E. Calculation is a dominant parietal function (Gerstmann syndrome).

q: A 49-year-old man with a chronic mental illness seems to be constantly chewing. He does not wear dentures. His tongue darts in and out of his mouth, and he occasionally smacks his lips. He also grimaces, frowns, and blinks excessively. Which of the following disorders is most likely in this patient?
explanation: A. Tourette syndrome has motor and vocal tics beginning in childhood. B. Akathisia is subjective restlessness with an inability to sit still. C. Orofacial involuntary movements (chewing, tongue darting, lip smacking) in a chronically treated psychiatric patient are tardive dyskinesia. D. Parkinson's disease gives tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. E. Huntington's disease has chorea with dementia and a family history.

q: The observation that levodopa (a drug used to treat Parkinson's disease) can cause mania and psychosis in some patients supports which neurochemical theory of psychiatric behavior?
explanation: A. Norepinephrine is not the neurotransmitter levodopa mainly raises. B. Levodopa is a dopamine precursor, so excess dopamine producing mania and psychosis supports the dopamine hypothesis. C. Glycine is not implicated by levodopa. D. Serotonin is not the primary neurotransmitter affected. E. Glutamine is not implicated.

q: Which of the following is a relative contraindication for ECT?
explanation: A. A space-occupying lesion with raised intracranial pressure is the classic relative contraindication (risk of herniation). B. ECT can be given safely in pregnancy with obstetric monitoring. C. Hypertension needs control before ECT but is not the standard listed contraindication. D. ECT is itself anticonvulsant; a seizure disorder is not a contraindication. E. Risk is highest within about 3 months of an MI; at 6 months it is much lower.

q: A 76-year-old man is diagnosed with dementia of the Alzheimer's type. Which of the following chemicals has been most commonly associated with this disease?
explanation: A. Peptide neurotransmitter changes (e.g., somatostatin) are less prominent. B. Epinephrine is not implicated. C. Dopamine is not the main deficit. D. Loss of cholinergic neurons (nucleus basalis of Meynert) with reduced acetylcholine is the best-known neurochemical change, hence cholinesterase inhibitors. E. Serotonin changes are secondary.

q: Column A (Mental State Examination). Select the section of the Mental State Examination where this information would be recorded. I'm always thinking about how nice it would be to close the door after every other minute. Sometimes I would keep checking to ensure it was closed, which would irritate my husband. But I can't help it! Even while at work, my mind is always thinking about that door.
options: Not part of mental state examination
explanation: A. Appearance: dress, grooming, hygiene and physical features, which does not match this description. B. Behavior: motor activity, eye contact, cooperation and psychomotor change, which does not match this description. C. Thought Form and Speech: rate, flow and logical organisation of thinking and speech, which does not match this description. D. Mood: the sustained emotion as reported by the patient, which does not match this description. E. Affect: the emotion as observed by the examiner (range, congruence), which does not match this description. F. Intrusive, recurrent thoughts and urges (obsessions) are recorded under thought content. G. Abnormal Perception: hallucinations, illusions and depersonalisation, which does not match this description. H. Cognition: orientation, attention, memory and abstraction, which does not match this description. I. Insight: awareness of illness and need for treatment, which does not match this description. J. Not part of mental state examination: items such as family history or lab results, which does not match this description.

q: Column A (Mental State Examination). Select the section of the Mental State Examination where this information would be recorded. "I see my dead grandmother staring back at me. Everyone else thinks I'm 'crazy', but I think I'm not!"
options: Not part of mental state examination
explanation: A. Appearance: dress, grooming, hygiene and physical features, which does not match this description. B. Behavior: motor activity, eye contact, cooperation and psychomotor change, which does not match this description. C. Thought Form and Speech: rate, flow and logical organisation of thinking and speech, which does not match this description. D. Mood: the sustained emotion as reported by the patient, which does not match this description. E. Affect: the emotion as observed by the examiner (range, congruence), which does not match this description. F. Thought Content: delusions, obsessions, preoccupations and suicidal or homicidal ideas, which does not match this description. G. Seeing a person who is not there is a hallucination, recorded under abnormal perception. The last sentence also reflects poor insight, but the main finding is the perception. H. Cognition: orientation, attention, memory and abstraction, which does not match this description. I. Insight: awareness of illness and need for treatment, which does not match this description. J. Not part of mental state examination: items such as family history or lab results, which does not match this description.

q: Column A (Mental State Examination). Select the section of the Mental State Examination where this information would be recorded. "I feel ecstatic! Where's the beer? Why does it look like we're in a funeral? Get out of the way! I need to throw a party!"
options: Not part of mental state examination
explanation: A. Appearance: dress, grooming, hygiene and physical features, which does not match this description. B. Behavior: motor activity, eye contact, cooperation and psychomotor change, which does not match this description. C. Thought Form and Speech: rate, flow and logical organisation of thinking and speech, which does not match this description. D. "I feel ecstatic" is the patient's own report of a sustained emotional state, which is mood (elevated). E. Affect: the emotion as observed by the examiner (range, congruence), which does not match this description. F. Thought Content: delusions, obsessions, preoccupations and suicidal or homicidal ideas, which does not match this description. G. Abnormal Perception: hallucinations, illusions and depersonalisation, which does not match this description. H. Cognition: orientation, attention, memory and abstraction, which does not match this description. I. Insight: awareness of illness and need for treatment, which does not match this description. J. Not part of mental state examination: items such as family history or lab results, which does not match this description.

q: Column A (Mental State Examination). Select the section of the Mental State Examination where this information would be recorded. "I need these tablets... Everything that is happening to me is real! I need them to ensure I keep my job as it keeps the illness away."
options: Not part of mental state examination
explanation: A. Appearance: dress, grooming, hygiene and physical features, which does not match this description. B. Behavior: motor activity, eye contact, cooperation and psychomotor change, which does not match this description. C. Thought Form and Speech: rate, flow and logical organisation of thinking and speech, which does not match this description. D. Mood: the sustained emotion as reported by the patient, which does not match this description. E. Affect: the emotion as observed by the examiner (range, congruence), which does not match this description. F. Thought Content: delusions, obsessions, preoccupations and suicidal or homicidal ideas, which does not match this description. G. Abnormal Perception: hallucinations, illusions and depersonalisation, which does not match this description. H. Cognition: orientation, attention, memory and abstraction, which does not match this description. I. The patient acknowledges illness and the need for treatment, which is insight (partial). J. Not part of mental state examination: items such as family history or lab results, which does not match this description.

q: Column C (Dementia). Select the most appropriate dementia/condition from the list. First described the condition that later assumed his name. He described a 51-year-old woman with a 4 1/2-year course of progressive dementia.
explanation: A. Alois Alzheimer described Auguste Deter (age 51) in 1906. B. Huntington's disease: an autosomal dominant disorder with chorea and caudate atrophy, which does not match this description. C. Lewy body Dementia: visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism, which does not match this description. D. Motor neurone disease: degeneration of motor neurones, which does not match this description. E. Multi-infarct Dementia: stepwise decline from multiple cerebral infarcts (vascular dementia), which does not match this description. F. Parkinson's disease: a movement disorder with tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia, which does not match this description. G. Pick's Disease: frontotemporal atrophy with disinhibition and personality change, which does not match this description. H. Binswanger's disease: subcortical small-vessel disease of the white matter, which does not match this description. I. Wernicke's encephalopathy: acute thiamine deficiency with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, which does not match this description. J. Wilson's disease: a copper-metabolism disorder (hepatolenticular degeneration), which does not match this description.

q: Column C (Dementia). Select the most appropriate dementia/condition from the list. Also known as vascular dementia, is presumed to be multiple areas of cerebral vascular disease, resulting in a symptom pattern of dementia.
explanation: A. Alzheimer's Dementia: the most common dementia, with plaques and tangles, first described by Alois Alzheimer, which does not match this description. B. Huntington's disease: an autosomal dominant disorder with chorea and caudate atrophy, which does not match this description. C. Lewy body Dementia: visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism, which does not match this description. D. Motor neurone disease: degeneration of motor neurones, which does not match this description. E. Multi-infarct dementia is the older name for vascular dementia. F. Parkinson's disease: a movement disorder with tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia, which does not match this description. G. Pick's Disease: frontotemporal atrophy with disinhibition and personality change, which does not match this description. H. Binswanger's disease: subcortical small-vessel disease of the white matter, which does not match this description. I. Wernicke's encephalopathy: acute thiamine deficiency with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, which does not match this description. J. Wilson's disease: a copper-metabolism disorder (hepatolenticular degeneration), which does not match this description.

q: Column C (Dementia). Select the most appropriate dementia/condition from the list. Also known as subcortical arteriosclerotic encephalopathy, is characterized by the presence of many small infarctions of the white matter that spare the cortical regions.
explanation: A. Alzheimer's Dementia: the most common dementia, with plaques and tangles, first described by Alois Alzheimer, which does not match this description. B. Huntington's disease: an autosomal dominant disorder with chorea and caudate atrophy, which does not match this description. C. Lewy body Dementia: visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonism, which does not match this description. D. Motor neurone disease: degeneration of motor neurones, which does not match this description. E. Multi-infarct Dementia: stepwise decline from multiple cerebral infarcts (vascular dementia), which does not match this description. F. Parkinson's disease: a movement disorder with tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia, which does not match this description. G. Agitation, confusion, fever, myoclonus and hyperreflexia after adding an antidepressant is serotonin syndrome (the key differences from NMS are myoclonus and hyperreflexia versus rigidity and bradyreflexia). I. Tardive dyskinesia: late-onset orofacial involuntary movements, which does not match this description. J. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: thiamine deficiency with confusion, ataxia and amnesia, which does not match this description.

q:
A 29-year-old male carpenter is brought to the Mental Health clinic by his mother for assessment. For the past 4 months, he has been noted to be talking to himself when alone, claiming that he is a CIA agent and is wanted by the Fiji Police. At times, his speech is irrelevant to the questions asked and doesn't make sense. He has not been able to go to school as he believes people want to kill him. (10 marks)
A. Suggest the most probable DSM diagnosis. (1 mark)
B. Provide reasons to support your diagnosis. (2 marks)
Upon further questioning, he reveals that he is unwell because of the curse put on his immediate family by their ancestors.
C. Discuss his level of insight. (2 marks)
D. Outline the pharmacological and non-pharmacological management of this patient. (5 marks)
answer:
**A) Most probable DSM diagnosis (1 mark)**
* Schizophreniform disorder (DSM-5), as symptoms have lasted 4 months, which is between 1 and 6 months
* Becomes schizophrenia if the illness (including prodrome) reaches 6 months

**B) Reasons for the diagnosis (2 marks)**
* Delusions: grandiose (CIA agent) and persecutory (wanted by police, people want to kill him)
* Hallucinations suggested by talking to himself when alone
* Disorganised speech: irrelevant, incoherent answers
* Duration of 4 months is under 6 months, and functional decline (cannot attend school)
* No prominent mood episode and no substance or medical cause described, so mood disorder and substance-induced psychosis are less likely

**C) Level of insight (2 marks)**
* Partial insight: he accepts he is unwell but attributes it to an external cause (an ancestral curse), not to a mental illness
* Fits level 3 of the classical scale: aware of being sick but blaming external or supernatural factors
* Consider cultural context: curse and ancestral beliefs are common explanatory models in Fiji, so explore with family before labelling the belief a delusion
* Insight is a treatment target; engage using his explanatory model to build adherence

**D) Management (5 marks)**
* Assess risk (to self and others, given persecutory beliefs) and admit under mental health legislation if unsafe or unable to consent
* Pharmacological: start a second-generation antipsychotic (risperidone or olanzapine) at a low dose and titrate, with an adequate trial of 4-6 weeks
* Continue for at least 12 months after remission in a first episode, then review
* If two adequate trials fail, switch to clozapine; use a depot if adherence is poor
* Monitor side effects (EPS, prolactin, weight, glucose, lipids, ECG)
* Non-pharmacological: psychoeducation for the patient and family
* Family therapy and carer support
* CBT for psychosis, supportive therapy and relapse-prevention planning
* Social and occupational rehabilitation (return to work, social skills training), case management and community follow-up
* Involve traditional or religious leaders if acceptable to the family, alongside medical treatment
* Screen for and counsel on substance use
explanation: Marks follow the allocation shown in each sub-question.

q:
A 26-year-old woman presents with a 5-week history of low mood, poor concentration, appetite and sleep, lethargy, and suicidal thoughts. She says that 10 months ago she had been feeling more talkative and energetic than usual and was more productive at work. This episode lasted about 3 weeks. (10 marks)
A) State the most probable DSM diagnosis. (1 mark)
B) Provide 4 reasons for your diagnosis in (A). (2 marks)
She is started on Sertraline and 1 week later has her dose increased to 150 mg per day. Within 8 hours of the change of dosage, she becomes agitated and appears confused, is sweating, and has a temperature of 39 degrees C. She appears to be stiff and tremors are noted on her hands.
C) What is the most likely underlying cause for her symptoms? (1 mark)
D) Outline the immediate management of this case. (3 marks)
E) Discuss the resumption of Fluoxetine in this patient. (1 mark)
One day, one of the nurses recognizes her and tells you that she plans to tell the client's boyfriend that she has been seen at the hospital.
F) Discuss what the nurse plans to do from a legal and ethical perspective. (2 marks)
answer:
**A) Most probable DSM diagnosis (1 mark)**
* Bipolar II disorder, current episode depressed (major depressive episode with a past hypomanic episode)

**B) Reasons for the diagnosis (2 marks)**
* Current major depressive episode: 5 weeks of low mood, poor concentration, appetite and sleep disturbance, lethargy and suicidal thoughts (5 or more symptoms for over 2 weeks)
* Past distinct period of elevated mood and energy (more talkative, more energetic) that was a clear change from baseline and observable
* The episode lasted over 4 days (3 weeks), meeting the duration for hypomania
* No marked impairment (she was more productive), no hospitalisation and no psychosis, so it was hypomania, not mania (which would make it Bipolar I)
* No substance or medical cause is mentioned

**C) Underlying cause (1 mark)**
* Serotonin syndrome from the SSRI dose increase (excess serotonergic activity)
* Supported by agitation, confusion, sweating, fever, tremor and stiffness within hours of the dose change

**D) Immediate management (3 marks)**
* Stop sertraline and any other serotonergic drug and admit for monitoring (vitals, ECG, temperature)
* Supportive care: IV fluids, oxygen and external cooling for hyperthermia (antipyretics are ineffective)
* Benzodiazepines (lorazepam or diazepam) for agitation, tremor and rigidity; avoid physical restraint
* Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) orally or by NG tube if symptoms persist
* For severe hyperthermia (above about 41 degrees C): sedation, neuromuscular paralysis with a non-depolarising agent and intubation, avoiding succinylcholine

**E) Resumption of fluoxetine (1 mark)**
* Do not resume it now: fluoxetine is another SSRI and its long half-life (norfluoxetine up to 2 weeks) would prolong serotonergic risk
* Wait until the syndrome has fully resolved before any serotonergic drug is considered
* Antidepressant monotherapy is also risky in bipolar II (switch to mania); prefer a mood stabiliser or quetiapine or lamotrigine
* If an SSRI is ever needed, give it only with a mood stabiliser, at a low dose with slow titration

**F) Legal and ethical perspective (2 marks)**
* The nurse's plan breaches patient confidentiality, a core professional, ethical and legal duty (and the Fiji mental health legislation protects patient information; verify the exact provision)
* Ethical principles violated: autonomy and privacy, non-maleficence (stigma, relationship harm, risk to a suicidal patient) and fidelity
* Disclosure is only justified with the patient's consent, a court order, or a serious risk to others, none of which applies
* Action: advise the nurse not to disclose, report the concern to the supervisor, and refer to the nurse's professional body if the nurse persists
* Document the incident and consider whether the nurse should step back from her care because of a conflict of interest
explanation: Marks follow the allocation shown in each sub-question.

q:
A 46-year-old male reports abdominal pain, chronic headaches, difficulty sleeping, and lack of energy. He fears that he has cancer somewhere in the intestine. He has experienced difficulty sleeping and a lack of energy for the past 12 years. He consulted several physicians (GPs and specialists) and all findings have been negative. The findings have only reassured him temporarily. His wife states that he is always preoccupied with his health. His current request is for sleep medication. (10 marks)
A. List and justify the 2 most likely differential diagnoses for this patient. (4 marks)
B. Describe the most appropriate management strategies. (4 marks)
C. How will you address the patient's request for sleep medications? (2 marks)
answer:
**A) Two most likely differential diagnoses (4 marks)**
* Hypochondriasis / illness anxiety disorder, as he has a persistent fear of having cancer despite negative investigations, only transient reassurance, multiple consultations and a preoccupation with health noted by his wife
* Somatic symptom disorder (or somatization), because of chronic physical complaints (abdominal pain, headaches, fatigue, insomnia) over 12 years with disproportionate thoughts and health-related behaviour
* Also consider (less likely): depression or GAD, given fatigue and insomnia, which can co-exist

**B) Management strategies (4 marks)**
* Build a therapeutic alliance, validate his distress and do not say it is "all in your head"
* Appoint one primary clinician with regular scheduled (not symptom-driven) visits
* Limit repeat investigations and specialist referrals once organic disease is reasonably excluded
* CBT (first line): challenge catastrophic beliefs, reduce checking and reassurance-seeking
* Psychoeducation for the patient and wife on the stress-symptom link
* SSRI (e.g., fluoxetine or sertraline) especially with comorbid depression or anxiety
* Treat comorbidities, relaxation training and graded activity

**C) Request for sleep medication (2 marks)**
* Acknowledge the problem and take a sleep history (depression, anxiety, caffeine, alcohol, pain)
* Explain why hypnotics are avoided: 12-year chronic insomnia, risk of tolerance and dependence, and drugs do not address the cause
* Offer sleep hygiene and CBT for insomnia
* If medication is needed, use short-term or low-dose options such as a sedating antidepressant (mirtazapine, trazodone or low-dose amitriptyline) rather than benzodiazepines or Z-drugs
* Review regularly
explanation: Marks follow the allocation shown in each sub-question.

q:
A 29-year-old female is brought to the emergency room by her anxious family members, who are worried about her vomiting and profuse diarrhea. On arrival, her pupils are dilated and there are signs of active lacrimation. Her blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg, her muscles are twitching, and has sodden skin. Her husband reports that these symptoms started 2 hours earlier. For the past few days, she hasn't been able to move much because of a knee injury, and during this time she has been increasingly anxious and restless. During the interview, she starts asking for an injectable painkiller that she has been using as advised by her previous doctors for the last six months. She has been yawning incessantly and has had a runny nose. (10 marks)
A. State the most probable DSM diagnosis. (1 mark)
B. Provide 8 reasons to justify your diagnosis in (A). (4 marks)
C. How will you treat a case of overdose with this drug? (5 marks)
answer:
**A) Most probable DSM diagnosis (1 mark)**
* Opioid withdrawal (after 6 months of prescribed injectable opioid analgesic)

**B) Reasons for the diagnosis (4 marks)**
* Six months of regular injectable painkiller (opioid) use with physiological dependence
* Abrupt reduction or loss of access (immobile, not obtaining the drug) preceding the symptoms
* Mydriasis (dilated pupils)
* Lacrimation and rhinorrhoea (runny nose)
* Yawning
* Sweating (sodden skin) and hypertension (180/100 mm Hg)
* Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea
* Muscle twitching and aches, with anxiety, restlessness and drug craving (asking for the injection)

**C) Treatment of opioid overdose (5 marks)**
* Airway, breathing and circulation first: clear the airway, give oxygen and ventilatory support or intubate if needed
* Naloxone (opioid antagonist) 0.4-2 mg IV, IM or intranasal, repeated every 2-3 minutes if no response (up to about 10 mg)
* Repeat doses or a naloxone infusion, because naloxone's half-life is shorter than that of many opioids, so respiratory depression can return
* Monitor in hospital for at least several hours, including vitals, pulse oximetry, ECG and glucose
* Look for co-ingestions (e.g., paracetamol, alcohol, benzodiazepines) and consider activated charcoal for a recent oral ingestion
* Treat complications (aspiration, hypotension, pulmonary oedema)
* After stabilisation, assess intent (accidental or deliberate), and arrange psychiatric and addiction follow-up
explanation: Marks follow the allocation shown in each sub-question.
